# Task 11 spec: re-split scenes at strong sequential emotion shifts

Owner decision (Martin, binding): a scene must not change mood halfway (calm, then the cyclone), because music only changes at scene boundaries. Split a scene ONLY where the dominant emotion changes strongly and persistently along the text. A simultaneous blend (bittersweet: calm with some sadness) is NOT a reason to split: it stays as the per-scene probability vector + intensity + tempo, and that model does not change. Pages inside a scene stay only for length. Avoid over-splitting.

Today: `pipeline/segment.ts` asks Meta for "one dominant mood" per scene and nothing checks it. Oz has 133 scenes; 28 have top final probability < 0.5, 17 have a top-2 gap < 0.15; lengths 53 to 845 words (median 269), 42 over 350 words.

1. New pipeline step `resplit`, after `classify` and before `cluster` (`npm run build:book -- oz --step resplit [--force]`; it also runs in the full sequence). It reads book.json and analysis.json and rewrites scenes.json and analysis.json.
2. Candidates: scenes with more than 350 words, or top final probability < 0.5, or top-2 gap < 0.15, or `final === null` is NOT a candidate (no vector, leave it). Scenes under 240 words are never split (both parts must reach the minimum).
3. Windows: cut the candidate into consecutive windows of whole paragraphs, greedily about 100 to 160 words each (a single long paragraph is its own window). Classify each window with the existing Jev client (same questions, model jev-1.14.0; extend `JevClient` minimally if you must, keep the `model` field in every request). Drop `unknown` and renormalize to the 8 ids with the existing helpers.
4. Split rule, pure and in `core/` (no network, unit-tested with fixed vectors). For a candidate boundary between windows, let L be the word-weighted mean vector of all windows on the left and R the same on the right (within the current segment). With a = argmax L, b = argmax R, a != b: margin = min(L[a] - L[b], R[b] - R[a]). Constraints: each side at least 120 words AND at least 2 windows or 120 words of one window (persistence: the new mood must hold, not spike in one short window). Pick the boundary with the largest margin; then recurse on each side (binary segmentation) with the same rule. Thresholds as named constants:
   - margin >= 0.30: split automatically.
   - 0.15 <= margin < 0.30: ambiguous, ask Muse (Meta, structured JSON `{ split: boolean, reason: string }`) with the text around the boundary (last ~2 paragraphs before and first ~2 after, plus both vectors). Muse decides only these.
   - margin < 0.15: no split.
   Tune these two numbers only if the Oz run shows clear over- or under-splitting, record the final values and why in the task doc. Target: a modest number of splits (a rough sanity range is 5 to 30 on Oz), never a split that leaves a part under 120 words.
5. New scenes: for each split scene, the FIRST part keeps the original id (old links and bookmarks keep working); later parts get the same id with a letter suffix: `c5s2b`, `c5s2c`. Unsplit scenes keep their ids and records untouched. One Meta call per split scene gives each part a title, summary and characters (structured output; English titles in the style of the existing ones). Then re-classify every new part with the full existing classify path (Jev, plus the Muse override on low confidence: reuse `classifyScene`, export it, do not duplicate it). Scenes stay ordered by start_n, cover each chapter with no gaps or overlaps, and never cross chapters: run `validateBookCoverage` before writing and fail loudly if it breaks.
6. Provenance: add `provenance.resplit` to analysis.json: thresholds, candidates count, windows classified, and one entry per split `{ from, into: [ids], at_n: [first n of each new part], margin, left: topId, right: topId, decided_by: "rule" | "muse", reason? }`, plus Jev and Meta usage and cost for this step (also add them into the totals). Idempotent: if `provenance.resplit` exists and no --force, skip. Keep segment and classify behaviour unchanged; `classify --force` must still work on the resplit scenes.json (it re-classifies the current scenes).
7. Dependents: rerun `--step cluster --force` (no network) so music-clusters.json covers the new ids (the data test requires it; the clusters file is a historical record of track prompts and nothing at runtime reads it). Check everything that depends on scene ids: the static routes `/leer/[sceneId]` (generateStaticParams reads analysis.json, so new ids get pages), the image API (`sceneIds` comes from the scenes; the scene image key is book + sceneId + textVersion + promptVersion; the text itself and textVersion do not change). There is no demo scene selector yet; if any hard-coded scene id exists anywhere in app/, server/ or core/ (outside tests), update it. Note in the task doc that a first part keeping its id could map to an older "Picture scene" image cached under that id; the Redis index is not installed in production yet, so no such image is live. Do not bump promptVersion.
8. Real run on Oz: `npm run build:book -- oz --step resplit`, then `--step cluster --force`. Spend target for the data pass: under USD 0.10 total (Jev is about USD 0.042 per 1M input tokens; Meta contributor is cheap). If it looks like it will cost more than USD 0.50, stop and report. Print a short summary: scenes before/after, splits with ids and the left/right top emotions and margins, decided_by counts, the new low-confidence counts (top < 0.5, top-2 gap < 0.15) and the word-length distribution (min, median, max, count > 350), and cost.
9. Tests: the pure split rule (auto split, ambiguous, no split for a blend where the top stays the same, persistence rejects a one-window spike, minimum 120 words per part, recursion yields two splits), id assignment (`c5s2`, `c5s2b`, `c5s2c`), and the step with fake Jev and Meta clients (coverage holds, unsplit scenes unchanged, provenance written, skip when already done). Existing data tests must pass on the new files.
10. Docs: update docs/contracts.md where it describes the pipeline or scenes, AGENTS.md product rules only if a rule changes (add one line: scenes split at strong sequential emotion shifts; blends stay in the vector), and BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md (task 11). Files stay under the size limit (pre-commit hook).

Run and report: `npm test` (count), `npx next typegen`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, `npm run check:isolation`, `npm run test:hooks`, `npm run check:size`, `node scripts/check-secrets.mjs --all`, plus the run summary from step 8.

Read text file `SECURITY.md`.
1|# Security
2|
3|## Report a vulnerability
4|
5|Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting on this repo. Do not open a public issue for a security bug.
6|
7|## What is in place now
8|
9|- Secrets live only in env vars. `.env.example` holds names, never values.
10|- A pre-commit scan blocks staged secrets: gitleaks when installed, plus the built-in scanner in `scripts/check-secrets.mjs`, which always runs.
11|- Scans cover all tracked paths except lockfiles, including `agent-logs/`, `public/`, and `.agents/skills/`. CI runs the built-in scanner with `--all` plus pinned gitleaks v8.28.0 with a hardcoded sha256, and GitHub Actions pinned to commit SHAs.
12|- `.gitleaks.toml` extends the default gitleaks config and allowlists only the known test placeholder strings, never paths.
13|- GitHub secret scanning and push protection guard the remote.
14|- Dependabot alerts track vulnerable dependencies.
15|
16|## Rules for later tasks
17|
18|Planned, not built yet. Each app task implements its share.
19|
20|- The BYOK Meta key is never stored server-side or in logs. It stays in the browser session (`sessionStorage`) and travels over HTTPS per request in a header.
21|- The owner `META_API_KEY` funds the public chat and images within the per-person quota and the global cap. Once a person's quota is used, they may bring their own key (BYOK). A BYOK request uses only the user's key and never falls back to the owner key.
22|- BYOK requests are still rate-limited per IP.
23|- Logged error objects hold no keys, tokens, or raw provider output.
24|- HMAC comparisons run in constant time.
25|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` for scripts and frames, and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` for images.
26|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Proxy tokens live only in env and travel as Modal-Key / Modal-Secret headers.
27|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after.
28|- The anonymous session cookie is signed with HMAC (`SESSION_SECRET`) and set httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax.
29|- IPs are stored only as salted hashes (`IP_HASH_SALT`) with daily keys.
30|- Quotas are strict per person: 15 questions and 5 images per day, counted by hashed IP and anonymous cookie, whichever runs out first. A global spend cap in Redis sits above them.
31|- Turnstile runs once per session.
32|- Errors never return stack traces or raw exception text.
33|- Book source files (epub, raw text) are never publicly served. Only processed public-domain JSON leaves the server.
34|- Security headers and a CSP live in `next.config.ts`.
35|- Input limits hold: question 500 chars, passage 600 chars. The server verifies each passage against the book text.

1|Ponytail ruleset by DietrichGebert, MIT, github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail (commit 09c434a). Level: full.
2|
3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.
35|
36|## Levels
37|
38|| Level | Behavior |
39||-------|----------|
40|| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
41|| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
42|| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |
43|
44|Run `ponytail-review` on your own diff before you hand it back.
45|
46|## Skills
47|
48|All pstack and ponytail skills live in `.agents/skills/`. Muse Code loads them when the workspace starts with `--trust-workspace`. Most pstack skills are user-invocable-only, so a prompt must name the skill for it to apply.
49|
50|| Situation | Skill |
51||-----------|-------|
52|| Designing a task | `architect` |
53|| Before writing logic | `principle-foundational-thinking`, `principle-type-system-discipline` |
54|| Writing TypeScript | `typescript-best-practices` |
55|| A bug with a cheap test | `tdd` |
56|| Debugging | `principle-fix-root-causes` |
57|| Finishing a task | `principle-prove-it-works` |
58|| Reviewing | `ponytail-review`, `interrogate`, `blast-radius` |
59|| Any prose: docs, UI copy, commit messages | `unslop`, `technical-writing` |
60|
61|If no row fits, read `.agents/skills/poteto-help/SKILL.md`, which maps situations to skills.
62|
63|`interrogate` is written for Cursor. Under Muse, run the same review with Muse subagents and `muse-spark-1.3` as reviewers.
64|
65|## Workflow
66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.
68|
69|A rescue by another tool happens only after those rounds. Log it in `RESCUE_LOG.md` with the date, the task, the tool, why Muse got stuck, what changed, and the commits. Rescue commits carry a `Rescue: <tool>` trailer and no Muse Code trailer; the hook skips them.
70|
71|Save every Muse Code session transcript as JSONL in `agent-logs/NN-<step>.jsonl`. Every commit carries the Muse Code co-author trailer, which the `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds. Update `BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md` with each task.
72|
73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader shows one scene at a time. Sub-pages split long scenes by length only. Music cues run on scene entry.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion.
91|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
92|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
93|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary.
94|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
95|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
96|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
97|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
98|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
99|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
100|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
101|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
102|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
103|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
104|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
105|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
106|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
107|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
108|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
109|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
111|
112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.
123|
124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|
130|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
131|
132|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
133|

3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.

Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.

112|## Security rules

114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

8|# TypeScript best practices
9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |

1|---
2|name: principle-test-behavior-not-implementation
3|description: "Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change."
4|disable-model-invocation: true
5|---
6|
7|# Test Behavior, Not Implementation
8|
9|A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. That includes return values, errors, state they can read back, and effects on systems outside the code, such as a request sent, a row written, or a message emitted. Implementation is what they cannot observe: private helpers, internal call order, intermediate data, and which internal collaborator did the work.
10|
11|Judge each test against two imagined edits:
12|
13|- **Break the behavior.** Make the code return a wrong value, skip an effect, or do the effect twice. If the test still passes, it proves nothing. The usual causes are an assertion looser than the contract, an expected value computed by the code under test, a restated constant or prompt string that never runs the code that reads it, and an assertion on data that the test built itself.
14|- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug.
15|
16|Keep a test that catches the first edit and survives the second. Rewrite or delete the rest. To write a test that does both, drive the code through its users' interface with a concrete input. Derive the expected value from the requirement, not from a run of the code. Assert what the contract promises, no less and no more.
17|
18|The contract decides, not the shape of the assertion. When "an empty cart never charges" is the promise, an assertion that the payment client got no call is behavior. Pair it with a case where the charge happens, so that the test shows it can see a call. The payload that a mocked external service receives is behavior, because that service observes it. A call to an internal helper is implementation, because no user can see it. An empty list is the exact answer when no record matches, and a hollow check when the test only needs some result. An exact error message pins wording that no caller reads. The error type that callers branch on is the contract.
19|
20|A test can pin an invariant instead of a call, such as a key that must exist in two tables or a compile-time type check. The invariant is the behavior.

4|disable-model-invocation: true
5|---
6|
7|# Test Behavior, Not Implementation
8|
9|A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. 10|
11|Judge each test against two imagined edits:

14|- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug.
15|

169|reach the scheduler. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
170|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
171|with the scene it belongs to.

173|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
174|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
175|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
176|becomes active and the override clears. Then a scheduled select draws
177|among the in-style tracks within `randomTolerance` of the best score,
178|keeping the current track when it is eligible, and switches to the
179|drawn track only once the current track played `minTrackSec`. A tick
180|passes the active scene back through the same draw, so a hold from

185|after that, dwell and the draw apply with the override track as the

187|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
188|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
189|skip override.

191|## Player

194|the latest switch, `canPrev`/`canSkip` with their handlers, volume and
195|mute with their handlers, the style list with the current style and its
196|handler, the end-of-track handler, and the playlist props

211|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
212|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.

214|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.

216|The bar is one sticky row, 56 px tall: the `Lectoria` wordmark left,
217|the player centre, the Chopin button and the source icon link right.

219|in the border token, and nothing touching the viewport edges. The inner

224|a mute icon button (`aria-pressed`, `aria-label` `Mute` / `Unmute`, the

226|(96 px) next to it, a style selector with `aria-label`
227|`Orchestra / Piano` and no visible label text listing only styles that
228|have tracks (hidden while fewer than two qualify), then the Chopin
229|button and the source icon link. The transport and mute buttons and the
230|source icon link are icon-only inline SVGs (`currentColor`, 32 px hit
231|area), quiet and neutral, Meta blue on hover and focus-visible, each
232|with `aria-label` and `title`; the source link reads `Music source
233|(opens in new tab)`. Previous walks the session history and restarts

235|in playlist mode; Next cycles same-emotion tracks in the style.

242|opus/catalogue suffixes from the track title, and the source is the
243|artist plus ` / <platform>` when the attribution names Musopen or
244|Jamendo and the artist does not already say it, dropped when it would
245|repeat the performer. The full manifest title plus the license and full
246|attribution sits in the `title` tooltip. On manifest failure the reader
247|still renders and the bar shows a short neutral note. UI motion stays
248|under 200 ms. Controls are real buttons and inputs with labels, visible
249|focus, and keyboard use. `app/player.tsx` keeps the audio engine,
250|transport, and bar layout; `app/player-controls.tsx` holds the style
251|selector and the playlist toggle; `app/music-prefs.ts` owns the storage
252|helper. The heading keeps `h2:focus:not(:focus-visible){outline:none}`
253|so mouse navigation shows no box while keyboard focus keeps its ring.

256|including the pure `displayTitle`.

258|`requestManualTrack` in `core/music-schedule.ts` holds a manual pick.

261|

264|the paragraph where the selection starts, `{ kind: "scene", bookId,
265|textVersion, sceneId }` names the scene. Validation is strict: known
266|book, matching `textVersion`, integer `n` inside the book, known
267|`sceneId`. Any other body is a 400 with a generic English message.
268|The client sends ordinals and ids only, never text. "Illustrate
269|scene" uses the scene id from the route.
270|
271|Responses (typed in `core/types.ts`): `{ status: "ready", url, cached,
272|caption }` with a Vercel Blob URL, never bytes; `{ status: "pending" }`
273|when another request holds the lock, in which case the client reposts
274|every 3 s up to about 2 minutes; `{ status: "error", code, message }`
275|where code is `quota`, `budget`, `unavailable`, or `bad_request` with a
276|friendly English message. Caption is the scene title for scenes and the
277|first words of the paragraph for passages, built server-side.
278|
279|The passage cache key is book plus start paragraph plus `textVersion`
280|plus `PROMPT_VERSION` (`v1`); the scene key is book plus scene id plus
281|the same versions. Both map to a deterministic Blob path
282|(`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An Upstash Redis
283|index maps key to Blob URL, so hits are one GET; on an index miss the
284|server lists by exact path prefix (head equivalent) before generating
285|and backfills the index.
286|A Redis lock per key returns `pending` to concurrent requests. Quota is
287|5 new images per person per day by hashed IP and signed cookie,
288|whichever runs out first; a shared spend counter in integer
289|micro-dollars sits under `SPEND_CAP_USD` (default 10). Failures refund
290|quota and budget and release the lock.
291|
292|## Chat api
293|
294|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
295|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
296|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
297|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
298|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
299|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
300|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
301|
302|## Quotas and budget
303|
304|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
305|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
306|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
307|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
308|the client, details stay in server logs.

94|`just-play-chopin`. A missing key parses as an empty list, and a v2
95|migration gives an empty list. Parse rejects duplicate playlist ids,
96|empty labels, non-array `trackIds`, and any `trackIds` entry that names
97|no track, with the playlist and the id in the message.
98|
99|## Selection
100|
101|`MusicSelection = { style }` is the session: `style` scopes every pick.
102|There is one mode only. Every scheduled select ranges over all tracks in
103|the current style and draws among the tracks with the scene emotion (or
104|the best same-style tracks when the emotion is missing) within
105|`randomTolerance` (0.05) of the best score, keeps the current track when
106|it is eligible, and avoids an immediate repeat otherwise. The style is
107|the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The default style is
108|the first listed style with tracks; a stored style with tracks wins. The
109|session persists `{ style, volume, muted }` in localStorage under
110|`lectoria.music.v1`. Old values with `mode` or `soundtrackId` load by
111|`style` alone and ignore unknown fields; a stored object without
112|`volume` or `muted` loads `volume: null` and `muted: false`. A bad
113|`volume` (not a finite number in 0..1) loads null and the player starts
114|at 0.8; a bad `muted` loads false. A stored style with no tracks falls
115|back to the default. Storage exceptions never break playback. Dwell
116|and min-track rules hold. The core never calls `Math.random`; the
117|reader injects it and tests pass a seeded stub.
118|
119|## Next track and style change
120|
121|`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order across the whole
122|style, wrapping and skipping the current, then the best same-style track
123|overall when the emotion is missing. A null scene cycles the style set
124|in id order. One track or none gives null.
125|
126|`requestStyleChange` picks the best match for the scene in the new style
127|by score. It never crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once
128|with the normal crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
129|mix toggle and no soundtrack-change button.
130|
131|## Playlist mode
132|
133|`SchedulerState.playlist` holds `{ id, index }` while a fixed playlist
134|plays. `enterPlaylist` switches at once to the first `trackIds` entry
135|with `crossfadeSec`, no dwell and no min-track rule. While it is on,
136|scene changes update the active scene but never switch, `requestNext`
137|and `noteTrackEnded` advance to the next entry in order and wrap from
138|the last to the first, and playlist tracks run to their end because the
139|player forces looping off. `exitPlaylist` clears the playlist state and
140|switches at once to the best match for the current scene under the
141|restored selection. The playlist is never persisted, so a reload returns
142|to emotion mode. The style selector stays disabled while it is on, and
143|the style list hides styles with only playlist tracks.
144|
145|## Similarity and config
146|
147|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
148|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
149|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1
150|(an all-zero vector gives an affinity of 0), `E` is the sum of
151|`sqrt(s_k * t_k)`, and the score is `weights.emotion * E` plus
152|`weights.intensity` and `weights.tempo` each for intensity and tempo
153|closeness. Scoring and ranking pass the resolved config weights in, so
154|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
155|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
156|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `dwellSec` (20),
157|`sceneEntryDwellSec` (5), `minTrackSec` (45), `crossfadeSec` (3), and
158|`randomTolerance` (0.05). Everything else reads from it. Ranking ties go
159|to the lower track id. Route entries use `sceneEntryDwellSec` as the
160|dwell override; scoring and overrides are unchanged.
161|
162|## Selection scheduler
163|
164|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The reader calls
165|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, and `noteTrackEnded`
166|with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable without
167|timers. The reader cues music on scene entry only: one `observeScene`
168|call per route id, gated by an id comparison, so sub-page moves never
169|reach the scheduler. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
170|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
171|with the scene it belongs to.
172|
173|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
174|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
175|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
176|becomes active and the override clears. Then a scheduled select draws
177|among the in-style tracks within `randomTolerance` of the best score,
178|keeping the current track when it is eligible, and switches to the
179|drawn track only once the current track played `minTrackSec`. A tick
180|passes the active scene back through the same draw, so a hold from
181|`minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a skip override stands: ticks
182|return no change while it is set, and only a new scene promotion
183|clears it. A switch reports the normal crossfade length (3 s, 0 s for
184|the first track ever). The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
185|after that, dwell and the draw apply with the override track as the
186|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
187|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
188|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
189|skip override.
190|
191|## Player
192|
193|`app/player.tsx` takes the track, `replayNonce`, the fade length for
194|the latest switch, `canPrev`/`canSkip` with their handlers, volume and
195|mute with their handlers, the style list with the current style and its
196|handler, the end-of-track handler, and the playlist props
197|(`playlistOn`, `playlistLabel`, `onTogglePlaylist`,
198|`controlsDisabled`). It owns two `audio`
199|elements, play state, volume, and the equal-power crossfade
200|(cos/sin gains over the fade time, driven by `requestAnimationFrame`).
201|It never uses the `loop` attribute. Volume lives in a ref, so the slider
202|never re-runs the track effect or touches `src`. A new track request
203|mid-fade cancels the pending fade and fades from the audible element to
204|the newest track. On load each track seeks to `startSec` once metadata
205|is available. Long tracks with `loop` true crossfade into the other
206|element playing the same track from `startSec` when `currentTime`
207|reaches `duration - fade`, where `fade` is the latest scheduler fade
208|length, or the config `crossfadeSec` when none was reported yet. When
209|`loop` is false the player reports the end and the scheduler picks the
210|next-best track excluding the ended one. Pause stops both elements and
211|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
212|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.
213|Audio starts only after the user presses play. Reduced motion is read in
214|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.
215|
216|The bar is one sticky row, 56 px tall: the `Lectoria` wordmark left,
217|the player centre, the Chopin button and the source icon link right.
218|The inner row is centered with 24 px side padding, one bottom hairline
219|in the border token, and nothing touching the viewport edges. The inner
220|max-width is 56rem, wider than the 65ch book column on purpose so the
221|full now-playing line fits at 1280 px. The player holds Previous,
222|Play/Pause, Next, the now-playing line (flexible space, `min-width`
223|16rem, truncated with an ellipsis, full line in the `title` tooltip),
224|a mute icon button (`aria-pressed`, `aria-label` `Mute` / `Unmute`, the
225|icon shows the muted state), a volume slider with `aria-label` `Volume`
226|(96 px) next to it, a style selector with `aria-label`
227|`Orchestra / Piano` and no visible label text listing only styles that
228|have tracks (hidden while fewer than two qualify), then the Chopin
229|button and the source icon link. The transport and mute buttons and the
230|source icon link are icon-only inline SVGs (`currentColor`, 32 px hit
231|area), quiet and neutral, Meta blue on hover and focus-visible, each
232|with `aria-label` and `title`; the source link reads `Music source
233|(opens in new tab)`. Previous walks the session history and restarts
234|the current track with no history, including the current playlist piece
235|in playlist mode; Next cycles same-emotion tracks in the style.
236|A `Just play Chopin` round image button (`/art/chopin-just-play-me.png`,
237|40 px, `alt` and `aria-label` `Just play Chopin`) appears only when
238|the manifest defines that playlist with tracks; it carries
239|`aria-pressed`, and while pressed it shows a 2 px Meta-blue ring plus
240|scale 1.05. The now-playing line shows `display title · composer
241|· source`: `displayTitle` drops quoted nicknames, key phrases, and
242|opus/catalogue suffixes from the track title, and the source is the
243|artist plus ` / <platform>` when the attribution names Musopen or
244|Jamendo and the artist does not already say it, dropped when it would
245|repeat the performer. The full manifest title plus the license and full
246|attribution sits in the `title` tooltip. On manifest failure the reader
247|still renders and the bar shows a short neutral note. UI motion stays
248|under 200 ms. Controls are real buttons and inputs with labels, visible
249|focus, and keyboard use. `app/player.tsx` keeps the audio engine,
250|transport, and bar layout; `app/player-controls.tsx` holds the style
251|selector and the playlist toggle; `app/music-prefs.ts` owns the storage
252|helper. The heading keeps `h2:focus:not(:focus-visible){outline:none}`
253|so mouse navigation shows no box while keyboard focus keeps its ring.
254|No user-visible emotion labels exist; ids stay as they are.
255|`core/music-credit.ts` builds the line as a pure function with tests,
256|including the pure `displayTitle`.
257|`core/music-history.ts` is the bounded history stack and
258|`requestManualTrack` in `core/music-schedule.ts` holds a manual pick.
259|
260|## Image api
261|
262|`POST /api/images` (Node runtime, `maxDuration` 120). Request is a
263|discriminated union: `{ kind: "passage", bookId, textVersion, n }` names
264|the paragraph where the selection starts, `{ kind: "scene", bookId,
265|textVersion, sceneId }` names the scene. Validation is strict: known
266|book, matching `textVersion`, integer `n` inside the book, known
267|`sceneId`. Any other body is a 400 with a generic English message.
268|The client sends ordinals and ids only, never text. "Illustrate
269|scene" uses the scene id from the route.
270|
271|Responses (typed in `core/types.ts`): `{ status: "ready", url, cached,
272|caption }` with a Vercel Blob URL, never bytes; `{ status: "pending" }`
273|when another request holds the lock, in which case the client reposts
274|every 3 s up to about 2 minutes; `{ status: "error", code, message }`
275|where code is `quota`, `budget`, `unavailable`, or `bad_request` with a
276|friendly English message. Caption is the scene title for scenes and the
277|first words of the paragraph for passages, built server-side.
278|
279|The passage cache key is book plus start paragraph plus `textVersion`
280|plus `PROMPT_VERSION` (`v1`); the scene key is book plus scene id plus
281|the same versions. Both map to a deterministic Blob path
282|(`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An Upstash Redis
283|index maps key to Blob URL, so hits are one GET; on an index miss the
284|server lists by exact path prefix (head equivalent) before generating
285|and backfills the index.
286|A Redis lock per key returns `pending` to concurrent requests. Quota is
287|5 new images per person per day by hashed IP and signed cookie,
288|whichever runs out first; a shared spend counter in integer
289|micro-dollars sits under `SPEND_CAP_USD` (default 10). Failures refund
290|quota and budget and release the lock.
291|
292|## Chat api
293|
294|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
295|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
296|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
297|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
298|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
299|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
300|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
301|
302|## Quotas and budget
303|
304|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
305|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
306|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
307|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
308|the client, details stay in server logs.
